facility_roles.quote: LHCf is an experiment dedicated to the measurement of neutral particles emitted in the very forward region of LHC collisions.

end.note: Ends at the LHC-wide start of Long Shutdown 3 (June 2026); LHCf only records LHC beam particles, so it cannot be active while the LHC is off.

intervals.label: operating
intervals.note: INSPIRE's date_completed field for this record is '9999', INSPIRE's own placeholder for 'not completed/ongoing' and not a real date, so it is not used. No source consulted gives LHCf's run-by-run schedule, so a single operating interval, ending at the start of Long Shutdown 3, is recorded instead of a richer run-by-run history.

end.note: CERN schedule: the LHC resumes operation in mid-2030; the rest of the CERN complex restarts in stages from mid-2028.

intervals.label: Long Shutdown 3
intervals.locator: home.cern/science/long-shutdown-3, item of 5 August 2026 "The LHC is being warmed up from near absolute zero to room temperature"
intervals.note: LHCf records particles produced in LHC collisions, so it is idle while the LHC is shut down; this is an inference, since no LHCf-specific statement about this shutdown was found. Status is shutdown, not upgrade. No source consulted says that LHCf's own detector is being modified in LS3. Start and end are the LHC-wide Long Shutdown 3 dates. CERN's 5 August 2026 item says 'The cryogenics team has been running the warm-up sequence since LS3 began on 29 June 2026' and that the stored helium is kept 'ready to be used again once the accelerator resumes operation in mid-2030'; CERN's 29 June 2026 article says 'The HiLumi LHC, scheduled to begin operation in 2030'. The end is a schedule value, not a reported event.
intervals.quote: Following its final physics run, the accelerator has been switched off to begin CERN’s Long Shutdown 3 (LS3) ... The HiLumi LHC, scheduled to begin operation in 2030

LHCf cannot record anything while its only beam source (the LHC) is off for LS3, so its operating interval ends at the start of Long Shutdown 3 and its status is shutdown.

physics_goals.locator: arXiv:2305.06633 Introduction (neutral particles, calibration of hadronic interaction models); home.cern LHCf page (particles thrown forward simulate cosmic rays, nearly zero degrees to the beam)
physics_goals.quote: In order to reduce the differences between models, it is necessary to have high-energy calibration data. ... the Large Hadron Collider forward (LHCf [17]) experiment was designed to measure the production of neutral particles at very high pseudorapidities
physics_goals.value: Measure neutral particles produced at very small angles in LHC collisions to calibrate the hadronic-interaction models used to interpret ultra-high-energy cosmic-ray air showers

summary.plain: LHCf uses two small detectors, 140 metres either side of CERN's ATLAS collision point, to study particles thrown almost exactly forward by LHC collisions -- data used to help interpret how cosmic rays create showers when they hit Earth's atmosphere.
summary.technical: Forward-physics/cosmic-ray-calibration experiment: two compact imaging sampling calorimeters (tungsten plates, plastic scintillator, position-sensitive sensors) at zero-degree collision angle, ±140 m from LHC interaction point 1, covering pseudo-rapidity > 8.4. Proposed and approved May 2004; operated (mainly during early low-luminosity periods of each LHC run) from first collisions (23 Nov 2009) through June 2026; off since CERN's Long Shutdown 3 began.

unique_capabilities.quote: This is possible since the laboratory equivalent collision energy of LHC is 1017 eV.
unique_capabilities.value: Compact imaging calorimeters at zero-degree collision angle, sensitive to the pseudo-rapidity range greater than 8.4, giving LHCf access to particle production kinematics equivalent to a laboratory cosmic-ray energy of 10¹⁷ eV
